cards.title: Map the Value Equation onto a physical product
cards.summary: Adapt Hormozi's four value drivers — dream outcome, perceived likelihood, time delay, and effort/sacrifice — to DTC by finding the specific ecommerce lever for each variable.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a physical product converts worse than a comparable competitor, or planning which offer elements to add first.
steps: State the dream outcome as the customer's end state, not the product: for a jacket it is looking good, staying warm, or both — the same SKU can carry different outcomes for different avatars.

Engineer perceived likelihood that the buyer will actually achieve that outcome: third-party reviews, demonstration content showing the outcome in use (the source cites a ~90-second Levi's video showing three ways to pair a jean jacket), and unboxing footage that demystifies what happens after checkout.

Compress time delay in two places: the purchase-to-delivery window (expedited or 1-day/2-day fulfillment) and the use window (for made-to-order or custom items, operationalizing faster tailoring or production).
Reduce effort and sacrifice inside the buying flow with saved-details one-click purchases and accelerated rails such as Shop Pay.
Confirm the four levers are not in conflict — a fast, easy, certain path to the exact outcome the avatar wants is the target state the source calls the ideal scene.
caveats: The source's worked example is a jacket and a jean jacket; adapt the specific content format to the product category rather than copying the video idea.

cards.title: Layer guarantees instead of relying on a money-back policy
cards.summary: Treat a standard refund policy as table stakes and add a second, implied guarantee layer such as delayed-capture Try-Before-You-Buy billing to further lower purchase risk.
cards.use_when: A store already offers returns and wants an additional risk-reversal mechanism that moves the conversion needle.
steps: Keep the conventional money-back or satisfaction guarantee as the baseline — the source describes it as nearly table stakes for physical products.

Add a second tier that removes risk before payment: the source points to Amazon's Try-Before-You-Buy, a roughly seven-day layaway where the card is charged only after the customer has had the item in hand.

Recognize that the delayed-capture model is itself a form of guarantee: it raises the buyer's certainty that they will like the item if they keep it, which inversely lowers the perceived chance of a bad experience.

Consider the operational consequences deliberately — delayed capture, return handling, and fraud exposure — before adopting it, and verify your payment processor's current support for delayed capture.
Combine with demystification content (unboxing, styling demos) so the customer already knows what to expect when the box arrives.
caveats: Delayed-capture layaway shifts cash-flow timing and return risk onto the merchant; treat it as a growth tactic, not a default.
Return-policy and payment-rail details change; check the current rules for your processor and platform.

cards.title: Use stock counts and time windows as separate scarcity levers
cards.summary: Scarcity (limited quantity) and urgency (limited time) are distinct ratchets — Amazon applies both, and drop models combine them.
cards.use_when: Planning launch mechanics, limited-edition releases, or a promo calendar for a DTC store.
steps: Apply quantity scarcity at the finest granularity available: Amazon shows units remaining per item and per size, so scarcity exists at every variant level.
Apply time urgency separately with a defined window, as in a lightning deal priced for a fixed period (the source's example is a 60-minute deal).
For drop models, combine both: print a fixed quantity (for example 100 units), release on a stated day, and make it first-come, first-served.
Decide which lever fits the offer's economics — a permanent SKU can still use live stock counts, while a limited run can also carry a hard end time.
Watch the interaction with the rest of the funnel: the source's contrast case is a competitor with no scarcity or urgency, where the buyer reasons they can simply come back next week.
caveats: Only display stock counts that are real; the source frames inventory-level scarcity as a conversion driver, not a scripted message.
Seasonal products lose urgency for buyers who see the item as year-round — segment or time the message accordingly.
cards.source_name: Applying $100M Offers to E-Commerce_ I'm Pissed.docx

cards.title: Stack zero-COGS digital bonuses on physical products
cards.summary: Attach informational assets — styling guides, usage protocols, pairing or combination guides — that raise perceived value without adding unit cost.
cards.use_when: Looking for ways to increase perceived value or AOV on a physical product without touching manufacturing cost or price.
steps: Identify the moment of friction right after purchase: the buyer's uncertainty about how to actually use the product to get the outcome.

Create a companion asset that resolves it — the source's examples are a styling/pairing video for apparel, usage instructions for kitchen or home gadgets, and dosing, timing, and combination guidance for supplements.
Match the bonus to the outcome and the avatar: the same product may be bought to solve different jobs, so guides can be produced for each use case.
Position the bonus as a perceived benefit of buying (included training) rather than a discount, so it lifts value rather than eroding margin.
Because the assets are digital, incremental COGS is effectively zero — the cost is production time, not per-unit cost.
caveats: The source does not give conversion metrics for bonus assets; treat the mechanism as a value lever, not a measured benchmark.

cards.title: Name products after the outcome and the search phrase
cards.summary: Outcome-explicit naming signals the dream outcome and matches how buyers search, while generic names like 'jacket' leave the value implicit.
cards.use_when: Writing or revising product titles on a PDP, marketplace listing, or ad creative for a physical product.
steps: Ask what job the buyer is hiring the product to do, then let naming follow from that job rather than from the category.
Choose the outcome words that match the avatar: for a warmth-seeking buyer, words implying heat belong in the name; for a fashion-forward buyer, words about lightness or style fit better.
Make the outcome explicit rather than implied — the source's contrast is a competitor listing it simply as 'jacket' versus a named outcome product.
Where the product is sold on marketplaces, prioritize the terms buyers actually search, as Amazon does, because a name matching the query reads as exactly what the shopper wanted.
Expect different avatars to respond to different names, and consider separate listings or variants when the same product serves distinct jobs.
caveats: Naming conventions and search behavior differ by platform; verify current listing rules and keyword tools before rewriting titles.

cards.title: Out-offer competitors with the same underlying product
cards.summary: Two stores can sell identical goods and convert differently purely because one has checked the value variables and enhancers the other has not.
cards.use_when: Building an offer differentiation plan when the product itself is not unique, or auditing why a competitor wins on a comparable item.
steps: Build the comparison explicitly across the levers: perceived likelihood (reviews and demonstration content), time delay (shipping speed), and effort (checkout friction and account creation).
Add the enhancer checklist: guarantees (including any try-before-buy), scarcity (live stock), urgency (time-limited offers), bonuses (usage guides), and naming (outcome-explicit).

Score both your store and the competitor on each line, using the source's contrast case — no demos, no guarantee, two-week shipping, forced profile creation, no scarcity, no urgency, generic name — as the weak profile.
Fix the cheapest, highest-leverage gaps first rather than redesigning everything at once.

Note that even a superior offer takes time to build if you use Amazon as the reference point; the source describes Amazon as having spent decades assembling these pieces, so treat it as a direction of travel.
caveats: This is a qualitative framework from the source's argument, not a controlled test showing a specific lift.

cards.title: Apply the value equation to purchase conversion, not lead conversion
cards.summary: The Value Equation is presented as the general mechanism behind purchasing decisions — value must be perceived in excess of price — and is argued to apply to physical products as well as services.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to translate a services-origin framework (Hormozi's $100M Offers) into a DTC or physical-product business.
steps: Treat the four variables as the universal layer: a buyer must want the delivered outcome, believe they can get it, get it fast, and expend little effort or sacrifice.

Translate each variable into physical-product mechanics rather than copying the service examples: reviews and demos for likelihood, shipping speed for time delay, one-click rails for effort, outcome naming for the dream outcome.
Treat scarcity, urgency, guarantees, bonuses, and naming as enhancers layered on top of the four variables to shift the value-price ratio further.
Recognize that the specific vehicle differs by category — services show a practitioner demonstrating a skill, physical products show the item in use and what happens after checkout.
Use this as the argument for charging more than a bare-listing competitor: the source's claim is that checking these boxes makes buyers willing to pay higher prices, not just buy more often.
caveats: This is the source's position, argued against a podcast comment that the framework does not apply to ecommerce; it is a framework argument, not a test result.
Service-business and B2B examples from the book are out of scope here; only the transferable logic is retained.
cards.source_name: Applying $100M Offers to E-Commerce_ I'm Pissed.docx
